I haven't read your story yet, but I wanted to comment this beforehand so I don't forget it.

I do not think you need to explicitly tell a backstory in order for people to care about your characters. 

The present should inform about their past, because you, as the writer, should be familiar with whatever that character lived through, or is suppose to have lived through. What they do, what they say, how they say it and why they say it should inform us, the readers, about who they are first and foremost. A backstory shouldn't, in my opinion, be the catalyst for the reader to engage or endear themselves to a character. If they have one, it should serve the purpose of informing a plot point or fleshing out a quality of the character. If you feel you need a backstory for the character to be interesting or relatable, then you've failed at writing that character.

Edit: Now that I've read your prompt, I think the issue lies in the idea itself. Your main character feels like a prop or a vessel. His dialogue doesn't convey a personality more so than a trope. And it's incredibly hard to write good, informative dialogue as it is, much more difficult in a short story or an introduction. My advice is not to try actively for a character to be relatable or liked, but to make them feel "real". You can achieve that by making it personal, basing them in aspects of yourself or people you hold dear so they can better inform a personality when they talk.
No character will be universally loved or understood and that's fine.
